The player behind the curtain

The music teacher asked us to listen once more, this time to the parts that ____2____. Without the familiar middle voice, I could hear where my violin line needed more support. The problem was real, but it did not make every possibility ____3____. We needed a new arrangement rather than a replacement person who could somehow arrive already ____4____. There were only two hours before the doors ____5____.

Our teacher found a simpler piece for three players. At first I disliked it because I had worked so hard on the original. Changing pieces felt like throwing away all that ____6____. Yet when we began, our weeks of learning to watch and listen to each other were still there. We did not have to start our cooperation from ____7____. We marked the new entries and tried the difficult turns slowly. By the final rehearsal, the music sounded different from our plan but no longer ____8____. I sent a recording to our friend, who replied with a reminder to enjoy the ____9____. Her reply made it easier to stop treating her absence as something she had done to ____10____ us.

Before going on stage, we told the audience why the programme had changed. They listened to what we could actually offer. The applause was warm, and afterwards our teacher praised our ability to ____11____ under pressure. She acknowledged the difficulty. We had been fortunate to have another score and enough guidance. Still, we had made good use of those ____12____. The following week our friend returned, and all four of us played the original piece together. I enjoyed it without believing it was the only worthwhile music we could ____13____. The concert had changed my sense of preparation. Practising a plan mattered, but so did building the skills that could survive a ____14____. We had lost one performance of a piece, not the value of working ____15____.
